extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Montaigne / Renaissance essays
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading / annotation of Michel de Montaigne's essay 'Of Vanity' (translated by Charles Cotton), extracting prescriptive observations and aphoristic guidance about writing, conduct, household management, spending, and government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid writing vainly about vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is, peradventure, no more manifest vanity than to write of it so vainly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cautions that writing about vanity can itself be an exercise in vanity; writers should be self-aware about the paradox of treating a vice as subject-matter and avoid producing self-indulgent work under the pretext of diagnosing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prate or write merely for words' sake
rubrics_metrics.description: “What, then, ought prating to produce, since prattling and the first beginning to speak, stuffed the world with such a horrible load of volumes? So many words for words only.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing that exists only to multiply words is worthless. Montaigne condemns idle scribbling and trivial pamphleteering that add volume without substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scribbling as social symptom — writing must serve vocation
rubrics_metrics.description: “scribbling seems to be a symptom of a disordered and licentious age.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive or idle writing indicates social and moral laxity; authors should ensure their work serves a real purpose rather than reflecting fashionable negligence of one's proper duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize significant remedies over trivial reforms in crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: “‘Tis no time to bathe and cleanse one’s self, when one is seized by a violent fever; it was for the Spartans alone to fall to combing and curling themselves, when they were just upon the point of running headlong into some extreme danger of their life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a society (or individual) faces serious danger, attention to trivial or cosmetic reforms is misplaced; fix root problems first rather than surface matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid half-hearted self-improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: “For my part, I have that worse custom, that if my slipper go awry, I let my shirt and my cloak do so too; I scorn to mend myself by halves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advocates consistency: either fully commit to correction or accept the state; piecemeal or hypocritical attempts at self-reform are condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing and books should be studied, not merely read
rubrics_metrics.description: Index line: “It is not a book to read, ‘tis a book to study and learn”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books merit deep engagement and study rather than superficial perusal; serious works require concentrated attention and reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid producing trivial pamphlets during larger social breakdowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that many write 'pitiful reformations about cloths, cookery, and law chicanery' while law and justice are absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In times of systemic collapse, focusing on petty reforms or novelties distracts from addressing pressing civic failures; authors and reformers should prioritize substantive civic questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate display of wealth; balance appearance and substance
rubrics_metrics.description: “We deprive ourselves of our own utilities, to accommodate appearances to the common opinion... All over-nice solicitude about riches smells of avarice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibit temperance between ostentatious display and miserly scrimping; neither extreme is virtuous—keeping or spending are indifferent except insofar as the will applies them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value order and cleanliness over abundance in household management
rubrics_metrics.description: “I love order and cleanliness... more than abundance; and at home have an exact regard to necessity, little to outward show.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good household governance prizes practical order and cleanliness rather than mere abundance or show; a host should aim for natural, unobtrusive hospitality instead of fussing or boasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not obsessively supervise servants or finances; allow some ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: “The most common security I take of my people is ignorance; I never presume any to be vicious till I have first found them so... I purposefully harbour a kind of perplexed, uncertain knowledge of my money.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne endorses a measured trust in servants and leaves some margin for their indiscretions, since obsessive control breeds avarice and torment; but this is balanced by preparedness and oversight in gross.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being consumed by small domestic thorns
rubrics_metrics.description: “The smallest and slightest impediments are the most piercing: and as little letters most tire the eyes, so do little affairs most disturb us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, repeated annoyances can cause more distress than big problems; cultivate patience and perspective so that minor domestic troubles don't dominate temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel should not spoil the pleasure of retirement; balance journeys with home life
rubrics_metrics.description: “I will not that the pleasure of going abroad spoil the pleasure of being retired at home; on the contrary, I intend they shall nourish and favour one another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travel enriches but must be balanced against the value of home and retreat; do not let the desire for novelty destroy domestic contentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reform by universal overthrow; beware of radical innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: “To undertake to found so great a mass anew, and to change the foundations of so vast a building, is for them to do, who to make clean, efface... Not so desirous of changing as of overthrowing things.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Radical attempts to remake institutions risk worse outcomes; prefer gradual, careful correction over ambitious wholesale revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: A good cure must restore, not merely excise the evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Surgeon metaphor: removing dead flesh is not enough; one must 'fill up the wound with better and more natural flesh, and to restore the member to its due state.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies (political or personal) should include constructive rebuilding; elimination of a problem must be followed by thoughtful restoration to avoid replacement by worse evils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public service is honourable but requires capacity and conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am of opinion that the most honourable calling is to serve the public... for where I see the weight that lies upon such employments, I perceive also the little means I have to supply it... and partly out of cowardice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serving the public is noble, but one should assess personal resources and conscience before assuming heavy public duties—abstain if unfit rather than perform poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer contentment in modest competence over futile ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne prefers living 'an excusable life' without bustle, to avoid becoming a burden to self or others; he'd rather be a good horseman than a good logician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value practical skills and comfortable competence tailored to temperament instead of pursuing status or abstract glory that doesn't suit you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom and existing institutions shape what government will work
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not according to opinion, but in truth and reality, the best and most excellent government for every nation is that under which it is maintained: its form and essential convenience depend upon custom.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political prescriptions should respect historical and customary arrangements; theoretical ideals may be impractical when imposed on established societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make small domestic details the subject of ostentatious hospitality
rubrics_metrics.description: “It ought insensibly to slide along, and to represent an ordinary current; and I think it unhandsome to talk much to our guests of their entertainment, whether by way of bragging or excuse.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosts should avoid boasting or excusing themselves about entertainments; natural, unobtrusive hospitality is preferable to ostentatious management of guests' impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of personal attention; distance can compose the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: “When absent from home, I divest myself of all these thoughts... My mind is easily composed at distance, but suffers as much as that of the meanest peasant when I am at home.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical or mental distance from entangling responsibilities can restore calm and perspective; remove oneself from immediate sources of vexation when possible.
